{{Short description|Second-largest eigenvalue lower bound}}
In [[spectral graph theory]], the '''Alon–Boppana bound''' provides a lower bound on the second-largest [[eigenvalue]] of the [[adjacency matrix]] of a <math>d</math>-regular graph,<ref>{{citation
 | last = Nilli | first = A. | authorlink = Noga Alon
 | doi = 10.1016/0012-365X(91)90112-F
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1124768
 | pages = 207–210
 | title = On the second eigenvalue of a graph
 | volume = 91
 | year = 1991| doi-access = free
 }}</ref> meaning a graph in which every vertex has degree <math>d</math>. The reason for the interest in the second-largest eigenvalue is that the largest eigenvalue is guaranteed to be <math>d</math> due to <math>d</math>-regularity, with the all-ones vector being the associated eigenvector. The graphs that come close to meeting this bound are [[Ramanujan graph]]s, which are examples of the best possible [[expander graph]]s.

Its discoverers are [[Noga Alon]] and [[Ravi Boppana]].

==Theorem statement==
Let <math>G</math> be a <math>d</math>-regular graph on <math>n</math> vertices with diameter <math>m</math>, and let <math>A</math> be its adjacency matrix. Let <math>\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n</math> be its eigenvalues. Then
:<math>\lambda_2 \ge 2\sqrt{d-1} - \frac{2\sqrt{d-1} - 1}{\lfloor m/2 \rfloor}.</math>

The above statement is the original one proved by [[Noga Alon]]. Some slightly weaker variants exist to improve the ease of proof or improve intuition. Two of these are shown in the proofs below.

==Intuition==
[[Image:Cayley graph of F2.svg|right|thumb|The [[Cayley graph]] of the [[free group]] on two generators <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> is an example of an infinite <math>d</math>-regular tree for <math>d=4.</math>]]

The intuition for the number <math>2\sqrt{d-1}</math> comes from considering the infinite <math>d</math>-regular tree.<ref>{{citation
 |last1 = Hoory |first1 = S.
 |last2 = Linial | first2 = N.
 |last3 = Wigderson | first3 = A.
 |pages = 439–561
 | title = Expander Graphs and their Applications
 | journal = Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.)
 | year = 2006
 | url = https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/~nati/PAPERS/expander_survey.pdf
 | volume = 43
 |issue = 4
 | doi = 10.1090/S0273-0979-06-01126-8| doi-access = free
 }}</ref> This graph is a universal cover of <math>d</math>-regular graphs, and it has [[spectral radius]] <math>2\sqrt{d-1}.</math>

==Saturation==
A graph that essentially saturates the Alon–Boppana bound is called a [[Ramanujan graph]]. More precisely, a Ramanujan graph is a <math>d</math>-regular graph such that <math>|\lambda_2|, |\lambda_n| \le 2\sqrt{d-1}.</math>

A theorem by Friedman<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Friedman|first=Joel|date=2003|title=Relative expanders or weakly relatively Ramanujan graphs|journal=Duke Math. J.|volume=118|issue=1|pages=19–35|mr=1978881|doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-03-11812-8}}</ref> shows that, for every <math>d</math> and <math>\epsilon > 0</math> and for sufficiently large <math>n</math>, a random <math>d</math>-regular graph <math>G</math> on <math>n</math> vertices satisfies <math>\max\{|\lambda_2|, |\lambda_n|\} < 2\sqrt{d-1} + \epsilon</math> [[with high probability]]. This means that a random <math>n</math>-vertex <math>d</math>-regular graph is typically "almost Ramanujan."

==First proof (slightly weaker statement)==
We will prove a slightly weaker statement, namely dropping the specificity on the second term and simply asserting <math>\lambda_2 \ge 2\sqrt{d-1} - o(1).</math> Here, the <math>o(1)</math> term refers to the asymptotic behavior as <math>n</math> grows without bound while <math>d</math> remains fixed.

Let the vertex set be <math>V.</math> By the [[min-max theorem]], it suffices to construct a nonzero vector <math>z\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}</math> such that <math>z^{\text{T}}\mathbf{1} = 0</math> and <math>\frac{z^{\text{T}}Az}{z^{\text{T}}z} \ge 2\sqrt{d-1} - o(1).</math>

Pick some value <math>r\in\mathbb{N}.</math> For each vertex in <math>V,</math> define a vector <math>f(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|}</math> as follows. Each component will be indexed by a vertex <math>u</math> in the graph. For each <math>u,</math> if the distance between <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> is <math>k,</math> then the <math>u</math>-component of <math>f(v)</math> is <math>f(v)_u = w_k = (d-1)^{-k/2}</math> if <math>k\le r-1</math> and <math>0</math> if <math>k\ge r.</math> We claim that any such vector <math>x = f(v)</math> satisfies

:<math>\frac{x^{\text{T}}Ax}{x^{\text{T}}x} \ge 2\sqrt{d-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2r}\right).</math>

To prove this, let <math>V_k</math> denote the set of all vertices that have a distance of exactly <math>k</math> from <math>v.</math> First, note that

:<math>x^{\text{T}}x = \sum_{k=0}^{r-1}|V_k|w^2_k.</math>

Second, note that

:<math>x^{\text{T}}Ax = \sum_{u\in V}x_u \sum_{u'\in N(u)}x_{u'} \ge \sum_{k=0}^{r-1}|V_k|w_k\left[w_{k-1} + (d-1)w_{k+1}\right] - (d-1)|V_{r-1}|w_{r-1}w_r,</math>

where the last term on the right comes from a possible overcounting of terms in the initial expression. The above then implies

:<math>x^{\text{T}}Ax \ge 2\sqrt{d-1}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}|V_k|w^2_k - \frac{1}{2}|V_{r-1}|w^2_{r-1}\right),</math>

which, when combined with the fact that <math>|V_{k+1}| \le (d-1)|V_k|</math> for any <math>k,</math> yields

:<math>x^{\text{T}}Ax \ge 2\sqrt{d-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2r}\right)\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}|V_k|w^2_k.</math>

The combination of the above results proves the desired inequality.

For convenience, define the <math>(r-1)</math>-ball of a vertex <math>v</math> to be the set of vertices with a distance of at most <math>r-1</math> from <math>v.</math> Notice that the entry of <math>f(v)</math> corresponding to a vertex <math>u</math> is nonzero if and only if <math>u</math> lies in the <math>(r-1)</math>-ball of <math>x.</math>

The number of vertices within distance <math>k</math> of a given vertex is at most <math>1 + d + d(d-1) + d(d-1)^2 + \cdots + d(d-1)^{k-1} = d^k + 1.</math> Therefore, if <math>n \ge d^{2r-1} + 2,</math> then there exist vertices <math>u, v</math> with distance at least <math>2r.</math>

Let <math>x = f(v)</math> and <math>y = f(u).</math> It then follows that <math>x^{\text{T}}y = 0,</math> because there is no vertex that lies in the <math>(r-1)</math>-balls of both <math>x</math> and <math>y.</math> It is also true that <math>x^{\text{T}}Ay = 0,</math> because no vertex in the <math>(r-1)</math>-ball of <math>x</math> can be adjacent to a vertex in the <math>(r-1)</math>-ball of <math>y.</math>

Now, there exists some constant <math>c</math> such that <math>z = x - cy</math> satisfies <math>z^{\text{T}}\mathbf{1} = 0.</math> Then, since <math>x^{\text{T}}y = x^{\text{T}}Ay = 0,</math>

:<math>z^{\text{T}}Az = x^{\text{T}}Ax + c^2y^{\text{T}}Ay \ge 2\sqrt{d-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2r}\right)(x^{\text{T}}x + c^2y^{\text{T}}y) = 2\sqrt{d-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2r}\right)z^{\text{T}}z.</math>

Finally, letting <math>r</math> grow without bound while ensuring that <math>n \ge d^{2r-1} + 2</math> (this can be done by letting <math>r</math> grow sublogarithmically as a function of <math>n</math>) makes the error term <math>o(1)</math> in <math>n.</math>

==Second proof (slightly modified statement)==

This proof will demonstrate a slightly modified result, but it provides better intuition for the source of the number <math>2\sqrt{d-1}.</math> Rather than showing that <math>\lambda_2 \ge 2\sqrt{d-1} - o(1),</math> we will show that <math>\lambda = \max(|\lambda_2|, |\lambda_n|) \ge 2\sqrt{d-1} - o(1).</math>

First, pick some value <math>k\in\mathbb{N}.</math> Notice that the number of closed walks of length <math>2k</math> is

:<math>\operatorname{tr}A^{2k} = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda^{2k}_i\le d^{2k} + n\lambda^{2k}.</math>

However, it is also true that the number of closed walks of length <math>2k</math> starting at a fixed vertex <math>v</math> in a <math>d</math>-regular graph is at least the number of such walks in an infinite <math>d</math>-regular tree, because an infinite <math>d</math>-regular tree can be used to cover the graph. By the definition of the [[Catalan numbers]], this number is at least <math>C_k(d-1)^k,</math> where <math>C_k = \frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}</math> is the <math>k^{\text{th}}</math> Catalan number.

It follows that

:<math>\operatorname{tr}A^{2k} \ge n\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}(d-1)^{k}</math>
:<math>\implies \lambda^{2k} \ge \frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}(d-1)^{k} - \frac{d^{2k}}{n}.</math>

Letting <math>n</math> grow without bound and letting <math>k</math> grow without bound but sublogarithmically in <math>n</math> yields <math>\lambda \ge 2\sqrt{d-1} - o(1).</math>
